<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS2" title="In Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.2 </span>Pipeline Specifications</span></a>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Mobile graphical user interface (GUI) agents driven by vision–language models (VLMs) perceive the screen as rendered pixels and choose actions from what they see, so they cannot reliably separate trusted interface elements from user-generated content. We present <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> (Mobile Injection of Realistic Adversarial GUI Examples), a pipeline that turns benign mobile screenshots into prompt-injection samples by placing attacker-controlled text into ordinary user-generated content regions, without modifying the agent, the application, or the operating system. <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> operates in three stages: a <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Localizer</span> identifies user-controllable regions on the screenshot, a <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generator</span> synthesises context-aware payloads and renders them in the application’s native style, and a <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Curator</span> moderates realism and balances the samples across applications, region types, and attack intents. A key challenge is that an injected screenshot must stay visually indistinguishable from genuine user content while still diverting the agent; we address this by separating the stages that control reach, realism, and distributional balance. On a 1,111-sample benchmark spanning ten applications and eleven attack intents, all five evaluated VLM agents are vulnerable, with attack success rates of <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23\%</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math>, and <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> scores higher on human realism ratings than the strongest prior attack (<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.02</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.52</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.52</annotation></semantics></math> out of <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>). We further find that per-sample realism and attack success are uncorrelated, so visual-quality filtering alone cannot reliably defend against this threat.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.28116v1/Motivation.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/501;" width="476" height="501" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Screenshot injection on a mobile GUI agent. Without an attack, the agent follows the benign goal of finding battery-life reviews; with a single injected user review instructing "Add to Cart", the agent is redirected to execute the payload.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rapid evolution of mobile graphical user interface (GUI) agents has created a new attack surface for adversarial manipulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez and Ribeiro, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greshake et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These agents are designed to automate interactions with mobile application interfaces by perceiving the screen primarily as rendered pixels directly rather than as a structured code representation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Therefore, agents cannot reliably distinguish trusted GUI elements from user-generated content such as comments or profile biographies. As a result, an attacker can inject malicious content that the application renders normally (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), thereby misleading the agent into performing insecure actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing prompt/content injection attacks for GUI agents either rely on a single manually crafted attack vector embedded at a predetermined injection site <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, or assume an overly permissive threat model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Zhang et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> overlays templated adversarial pop-ups onto desktop and web environments such as OSWorld and VisualWebArena. EIA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> relies on editable HyperText Markup Language (HTML) structure to inject malicious elements at the Document Object Model (DOM) level. These approaches are tied to the web setting and are therefore inapplicable to screenshot-only mobile agents. Other approaches, such as backdoor attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, assume the adversary can tamper with training data or model weights before deployment, which overstates attacker capability and tests the training stage rather than runtime behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we design <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>, a screenshot injection attack against mobile GUI agents. We consider a realistic runtime threat model in which attackers can inject malicious instructions only through ordinary user-generated content regions without modifying the agent, application or the underlying operating system. Our key insight is that such user-controlled regions are already present in benign screenshots, rendered in the application’s native style, and thus serve as natural injection sites that require no access to the underlying application or its DOM. Building on this, <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> operates directly on screenshots to generate GUI injections across diverse applications while preserving the visual and semantic consistency of the surrounding interface.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> realizes this through a three-stage pipeline that transforms benign mobile screenshots into labeled visual screenshot-injection samples (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Given a screenshot, the <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Localizer</span> identifies user-controllable regions by iteratively tightening coarse vision–language model (VLM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> predictions with optical character recognition (OCR) guidance. The <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generator</span> then produces context-aware payloads for each region and attack intent, and injects them via style-preserving text rendering. Lastly, the <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Curator</span> applies post-render VLM moderation with retry-based correction and balances the dataset across applications, region types, and attack intents. Together, these stages yield an attack that reflects realistic attacker capabilities and is deployable without privileged access to the target system.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>’s attack success rate (ASR) by conducting a comprehensive experimental study over 353 unique <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\textit{raw\_image},\textit{user\_goal})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">raw_image</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">user_goal</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\textit{raw\_image},\textit{user\_goal})</annotation></semantics></math> pairs spanning 10 popular mobile applications, generating a total of 1,111 attack instances across diverse user-interface (UI) states and balanced attack intents. We assess generality and effectiveness across five VLM backbone models, finding that <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> achieves consistent attack success across models, with ASR ranging from 23.0% to 30.2%, and reaching its peak performance (30.2%) on GPT-4o-mini. Across applications, <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> maintains better cross-app robustness, with ASR exceeding 19% under all evaluated settings and attack intents. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, <span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> achieves higher perceived realism without sacrificing attack success, producing screenshots closer to user-generated content. Our ablation further shows that these properties are attributable to distinct pipeline stages that separately control reach, realism, and distributional balance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We characterise a runtime threat model for visual-channel prompt injection against mobile GUI agents—attackers control only ordinary user-generated content regions, with no modifications to the agent, application, or operating system—and specify the intent-to-action mapping and evaluation conditions (§<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Threat Model and Problem Setup ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:1.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>, a three-stage attack methodology (Localizer, Generator, Curator) that automatically synthesises visually plausible, context-aware injection samples on mobile GUIs from benign screenshots, without per-app code or agent fine-tuning (§<a href="#S3" title="3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:1.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform an empirical security study across five VLM-based GUI agents, ten applications, and eleven attack intents (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), and report two mechanism findings: visual plausibility is uncorrelated with attack success (<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.03</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-0.03</annotation></semantics></math>), so visual-quality filtering alone cannot reliably defend against this attack class;
and attack success is driven more by the attack intent than by model identity or visual realism, with intents consistently forming three exploitation levels across agents.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:1.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We release our code and the full benchmark to support reproducible evaluation of VLM-based GUI agents.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt injection in the large language model (LLM)–agent stack.</span>
Prompt injection has expanded from a direct text-channel threat against LLMs into a system-level concern for LLM-based agents.
Early work showed that adversarial instructions placed in user prompts can hijack model behavior or extract hidden prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez and Ribeiro, 2022</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greshake et al. (2023)</a></cite> then introduced the indirect variant, in which malicious instructions are embedded in third-party data that the model later retrieves.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite> formalized this attack space and benchmarked several injection and defense strategies, while InjecAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and AgentDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Debenedetti et al., 2024</a>)</cite> extend the analysis to tool-using agents that consume untrusted tool outputs.
All of these benchmarks operate over text and tool-output channels, and their attacker-intent taxonomies are organized around tool-side outcomes such as data exfiltration or unauthorized application programming interface (API) calls rather than the UI action space of a GUI agent. Different from existing work, we target the visual perception channel of mobile GUI agents, where injected content reaches the agent through rendered screenshots rather than text streams.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial attacks on GUI agents.</span>
Existing work mainly focuses on generating attacks on the visual or environmental inputs for web and mobile agents.
WebInject formulates prompt injection as a pixel-level optimization over rendered pages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite> instrument real Android apps with third-party content to measure deployment-realistic robustness, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> build GhostEI-Bench on Android emulators. and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al. (2025)</a></cite> expose backdoor vulnerabilities in VLM-based mobile GUI agents.
None of these works automates the localization of potential user-controllable injection regions in rendered mobile screenshots, and their payloads are hand-crafted distractors rather than goal-conditioned, context-aware lures.
We instead explore <em id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">automated, content-level</em> payload generation for mobile GUI injection on rendered screenshots. Our work aims to produce injection attacks that are visually plausible, context-aware, and balanced across applications, region types, and attack intents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mobile GUI agents and benchmarks.</span>
Existing VLM-based mobile GUI agents fall into two architectural classes: native GUI agents such as UI-TARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Mobile-Agent-v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> predict executable actions directly from screenshots, while general-purpose VLMs such as the Qwen-VL family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> serve as backbones behind a GUI action wrapper.
We evaluate the latter class because native GUI agents require local graphics processing unit (GPU) hosting (§<a href="#S6" title="6 Limitations ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).
Existing GUI-agent benchmarks (WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, VisualWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and AndroidWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) measure benign task completion rather than adversarial robustness, and are constructed through static task collection rather than generative procedures that balance the distribution over inputs and target behaviors.
Multimodal jailbreak attacks on aligned VLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shayegani et al., 2024</a>)</cite> are adjacent but distinct: they target language output rather than the action policy of a GUI agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.28116v1/Methodology.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/304;" width="452" height="304" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>End-to-end pipeline of <span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>: the Localizer (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Adaptive Injection Point Localization (Localizer) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) marks user-controllable regions, the Generator (§<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Context-Aware Payload Generation (Generator) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) writes a context-aware payload per region and intent, and the Curator (§<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Realism Moderation and Balanced Sampling (Curator) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) filters render artefacts and balances the surviving samples. The bottom strip threads one running example through all three stages.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>, a three-stage pipeline that turns a benign mobile screenshot into visual prompt-injection samples for benchmarking VLM-based GUI agents.
Given a base screenshot <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and attack intents <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, it produces for each <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,i_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,i_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> an injected screenshot <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> that lures the agent into an attacker-specified action while it believes it is pursuing a benign user goal.
The three stages run in sequence (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), each securing a property that no single model call reliably delivers: the <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Localizer</span> a plausible attack surface, the <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generator</span> local visual and semantic consistency, and the <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Curator</span> a balanced, clean dataset.
Each subsection (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Adaptive Injection Point Localization (Localizer) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>–§<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Realism Moderation and Balanced Sampling (Curator) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) opens with the failure mode that motivates it; a high-level pipeline specification is in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Threat Model and Problem Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A mobile GUI agent maps a screenshot and a user goal to a concrete action from a fixed set of six UI primitives—tap, text entry, swipe, back, wait, and task termination. The attacker can inject malicious content into user-controllable surfaces (e.g., comments or messages) but cannot modify the agent, app, or OS. The attacker’s goal is to induce the agent to execute an unintended action aligned with the injected malicious intent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following prior work that organises prompt injection by the attacker’s intended outcome <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we group attacker-preferred outcomes into 11 <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attack intents</em> (detailed in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>), each mapping to one action in the agent’s action space. For instance, <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tapping</span> the injected comment element.
An attack succeeds when, on an injected screenshot, the agent performs the attacker-intended action instead of the correct action implied by the benign user goal. The fraction of injected screenshots satisfying this condition is reported as the ASR.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> must therefore automatically construct a visually realistic, large-scale benchmark spanning applications, region types, and intents, so that both attack success and benign performance are measured on the same agent using identical screenshots.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Adaptive Injection Point Localization (Localizer)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Localizer returns a typed, tightly bounded set of injection regions, each drawn from a user-controllable surface such as review body, comment, post body, profile field.
Since a single VLM pass often merges UI regions, selects implausible targets and misses user-content cards, we adopt a multi-stage localization pipeline.
In detail, a VLM emits coarse candidates tagged with region type and a user-controllability flag, and the pipeline drops regions marked not user-controllable. An OCR pass (EasyOCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">JaidedAI, 2024</a>)</cite>) then tightens each candidate box to its detected text region and discards candidates without high-confidence text. Finally, an independent VLM moderator, following the self-refinement pattern of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al. (2023)</a></cite>, reviews an annotated overlay of the current candidates and emits per-issue repairs from {drop, tighten, extend, add} until no severe issue remains or an iteration cap is reached. The region-type vocabulary, the severity rubric (distinct from the Curator’s in §<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Realism Moderation and Balanced Sampling (Curator) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>), and the iteration cap are in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Context-Aware Payload Generation (Generator)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Generator turns each localized region and attack intent into a concrete payload that lures the agent toward the attacker’s chosen action while reading as ordinary content for that UI region. A single one-step VLM call typically collapses the user goal and the lure into the same target, or emits an explicit instructional payload such as “TAP HERE NOW.” The Generator therefore separates three steps. A VLM first synthesises a one-sentence benign user goal subject to an <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ambiguity rule</em>: at least one user-controllable region must remain a plausible competing target, so that agent failure reflects susceptibility to injection rather than unrelated perception difficulty. The payload generator then conditions on the screenshot, region crop, region type, synthesised goal, and target intent; a pre-render LLM reviewer regenerates the payload (up to three times) when it duplicates the user goal, misses the intent’s semantic role, or reads as an explicit command, and samples still failing after three attempts are dropped before rendering. A context-preserving renderer finally inpaints the payload into the injection region: we prompt <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-image-2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>)</cite>, an image-editing model, to render the payload text in the application’s native style and leave the rest of the screenshot unchanged, matching the surrounding typography for text regions and producing a native-looking, subject-preserving in-image caption for media regions. Goal-synthesis prompt, reviewer rejection taxonomy, and renderer parameters are in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Realism Moderation and Balanced Sampling (Curator)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Curator, the final stage in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, filters per-sample render artefacts and balances the final distribution. Filtering alone yields cleaner sets that remain skewed toward common region types and easy intents, and balancing alone yields evenly distributed but visually noisy sets, so the Curator applies both. A post-render VLM moderator scores each render against an artefact taxonomy and labels artefacts by severity (overflow, truncation, background or font mismatch, glyph leakage, layout overlap); samples pass—with annotations for low- or medium-severity issues—unless a high-severity issue triggers re-rendering with the moderator’s feedback, up to an iteration cap. Three balancing mechanisms then act on the surviving samples. A <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pre-generation allocator</em> assigns each base screenshot a sample budget that begins uniform over (intent, region-type) combinations and reweights toward under-represented combinations after each batch of moderated samples. A <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-generation trim</em> subsamples over-represented combinations. A one-pass <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coverage repair</em> regenerates samples for Localizer injection points that have no surviving sample after moderation. The pipeline outputs a filtered, balanced set of injected screenshots paired with attack metadata (intent label, region type, injection bounding box). Severity definitions, allocation parameters, the full artefact taxonomy, and an example annotated overlay are in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> through three research questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1 (Generality and determinants)</span>: is visual injection through plausible user-generated content a structural vulnerability of VLM-based mobile GUI agents, and what predicts per-sample success?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2 (Stealth)</span>: can visual-quality filtering, the most natural runtime defense against rendered injections, catch <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> attacks?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3 (Pipeline contribution)</span>: does each pipeline stage (Localizer, Generator, Curator) contribute a distinct property of the attack distribution?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dataset.</span> We construct the evaluation dataset from ten widely used mobile applications across five categories. For each we collect up to ten base screenshots across different UI states, avoiding near-duplicate layouts and requiring at least one plausible user-controllable region, for <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96</annotation></semantics></math> base screenshots in total. <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> expands these into <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}111" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,111</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}111</annotation></semantics></math> injected samples balanced across attack intents and action types, of which a fixed-seed <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math>-sample stratified subset is reserved for the RQ3 ablation. The application list, per-app counts, and intent-to-action mapping are in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models.</span> We evaluate five VLM-based GUI action-prediction agents behind a unified interface: the closed-weight <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span> (OpenAI API) and four open-weight models served via SiliconFlow—<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GLM-4.5V</span> and the Qwen3-VL family at 8B, 30B-A3B, and 32B. Each agent receives the same input—a screenshot and a benign task instruction—and emits a structured GUI action, with the system prompt, decoding parameters, and output format held fixed across <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> and all baselines (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS6" title="B.6 Inference Configuration ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.6</span></a>). We exclude native GUI-specialised agents that require local GPU hosting (§<a href="#S6" title="6 Limitations ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">21</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">43</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">25</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">25</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">24</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">25</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">30</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">20</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">35</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.7.12" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.7.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">27</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S4.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Every evaluated agent is vulnerable (aggregate ASR <math id="S4.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>23.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.T1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>); per-application risk tracks user-generated-content surface area.</span> Per-app ASR (%) on the <math id="S4.T1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}111" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,111</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}111</annotation></semantics></math>-sample main set; rightmost column is the per-model aggregate (<math id="S4.T1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> Wilson CIs; full set in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). <span id="S4.T1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span>/<span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underline</span> = model’s most/second-most vulnerable app. WA WhatsApp, Amaz Amazon, Spot Spotify, Tel Telegram, TikT TikTok.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation metric.</span> Each evaluation sample is a triple <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s^{\prime},g,a^{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s^{\prime},g,a^{\star})</annotation></semantics></math>: an injected screenshot <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> (§<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Context-Aware Payload Generation (Generator) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), a synthesised benign user goal <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, and the attacker-specified target action <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>. The attack succeeds when agent <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>’s action on <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s^{\prime},g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s^{\prime},g)</annotation></semantics></math> equals <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> rather than the action implied by <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>; our primary metric is the ASR over the evaluation set <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{(s^{\prime},g,a^{\star})\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbbm{1}[f(s^{\prime},g)=a^{\star}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ASR</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{(s^{\prime},g,a^{\star})\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbbm{1}[f(s^{\prime},g)=a^{\star}]</annotation></semantics></math>. Two secondary metrics support later analyses: <em id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Realism</em>, the mean 5-point human Likert over the four UI-quality criteria of Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Realism Rubric ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> (LLM judge under measured agreement), and <em id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Coverage</em>, the breadth of injection points and action categories reached.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines and ablations.</span> We compare <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> against <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AgentHazard</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (AH), re-rendering its released <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">adv_str</span> payloads onto its own screenshots in <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>’s render style and scoring all five agents under the same per-intent ASR (§<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Threat Model and Problem Setup ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>). The two releases share no base screenshots, so the comparison is at the application level, on the Spotify/Temu/X overlap (sample counts in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Per-RQ Procedure ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>). <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GhostEI</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> releases hand-written prompts without rendered screenshots and is excluded. Three internal ablations (<math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>Loc, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>Gen, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>Cur) each disable one pipeline stage (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Ablation Variants ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Protocol.</span> RQ1 and RQ2 use the full <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}111" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,111</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}111</annotation></semantics></math>-sample main set evaluated by all five agents. RQ3 uses the <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math>-sample stratified ablation subset with two agents (<span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span> and Qwen3-VL-32B) fixed after RQ1 to bound inference cost. Full per-RQ procedures are in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Per-RQ Procedure ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>RQ1: Generality and determinants</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All five evaluated agents are vulnerable, and the cross-model spread is small relative to the cross-application and cross-intent spreads. We establish this on the <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}111" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,111</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}111</annotation></semantics></math>-sample main set. Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports per-application ASR (the same matrix appears as a heatmap in Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). We read off three determinants of per-sample success in decreasing order of induced ASR spread—attack intent, application surface, and model identity—then turn to coverage and the comparison with the strongest prior attack on raw ASR.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Every evaluated agent is vulnerable.</span> Aggregate ASR is confined to a <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>23.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> band across the five backbones—<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span> highest and Qwen3-VL-32B lowest—regardless of whether each is closed- or open-weight, dense or mixture-of-experts, and the 95% confidence intervals of the top three overlap (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). The narrow spread shows that visual-channel GUI injection is not specific to a single model family, alignment regime, or deployment style; it appears to be a property of the VLM-grounded GUI agent paradigm at currently deployed sizes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack intent partitions into three exploitation tiers.</span> The eleven intents fall into three regimes defined by the mechanism each exploits, and the tiers are stable across models (per-intent ASR in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). <em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Temporal and attention lures</em> (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_wait</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">external_link</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_answer</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_swipe</span>; up to <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="88\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>88</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">88\%</annotation></semantics></math>) exploit instruction-following on procedural cues: phrases such as “please wait…” or “tap here to continue” read as natural guidance, and the bias toward procedural compliance carries the attack—most strongly for the best instruction-followers (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_swipe</span> swings <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> across models). <em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Action redirection within the same interface</em> (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click_elsewhere</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">follow_user</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">enable_permission</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_terminate</span>; <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>17</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>26</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26\%</annotation></semantics></math>) exploits semantic ambiguity between attacker- and user-preferred targets, and lands less often than the clearest lures because the user goal supplies an opposing signal. <em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.13" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Interaction-primitive manipulation</em> (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_back</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">induce_long_press</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">inject_text</span>; lowest tier) targets interactions that ordinary user-generated content rarely cues—a back gesture, long press, or writeable field—so the attack lacks a benign-looking template to hide behind (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">inject_text</span> is bounded by the rarity of fillable fields, not agent resistance). The structure is therefore a property of the intent–mechanism mapping rather than of any specific agent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Per-application ASR tracks user-generated-content surface area.</span> Applications dominated by user-generated-content cards expose the most attack surface (Amazon, X, Facebook, and Temu, all <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 30\%</annotation></semantics></math>), while those dominated by chat bubbles, short captions, or media playback expose less (TikTok, WhatsApp, Telegram, Spotify) and force the Localizer onto narrower targets. The actionable per-application risk factor for app designers and platform reviewers is therefore the visible user-generated-content surface area, not the choice of underlying model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model identity is the weakest determinant.</span> Within the Qwen3-VL family, aggregate ASR decreases monotonically with parameter count, from <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="28.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>28.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28.9\%</annotation></semantics></math> at 8B to <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>23.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> at 32B. This <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 6</annotation></semantics></math> percentage-point (pp) spread is consistent but small beside the <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 23" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 23</annotation></semantics></math>pp cross-application and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 82" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>82</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 82</annotation></semantics></math>pp cross-intent spreads above, so scaling within a family is at best a partial mitigation: no agent is uniformly hard to attack, and the exploitable surface is set by intent rather than scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The pipeline covers a broad slice of the attack surface.</span> From the same base screenshots, <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> reaches a wide slice of the GUI attack surface: the final set is near-uniform over the eleven intents (normalised entropy <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.990" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.990</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.990</annotation></semantics></math>, from the Curator’s balance-trim) and covers all four coarse action categories (<span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">confirm</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">navigate</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">type</span>), whereas AgentHazard covers only three—missing <span id="S4.SS2.p6.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">type</span>—under the same denominator (Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>; Localizer funnel in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Pipeline Specifications ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>). Two shortfalls remain, both the cost of expanding each base into controlled variants rather than sampling independently authored screens: lower Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) screenshot dispersion and lower goal-text cluster entropy than the hand-authored baselines (§<a href="#S6" title="6 Limitations ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>; numbers in Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-method comparison: <span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> trades raw ASR for plausibility.</span> On the three-application overlap (Spotify, Temu, X), AgentHazard’s paired attacks reach <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="21" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>21</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21</annotation></semantics></math>pp higher ASR than <span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>. <span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> is thus not the most aggressive attack per sample here; RQ2 shows the plausibility gain it trades for, RQ3 the stage that produces it. Per-cell ASR and two overlap caveats—a narrower intent space and AH’s broader threat model—are in Appendices <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Result Tables ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> and <a href="#A2.SS8" title="B.8 Cross-Method Comparison: AgentHazard Paired Set ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>RQ2: Stealth</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Visual-quality filtering does not work as a runtime defense against <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>. We establish this with a 200-sample paired human study—100 <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> and 100 AgentHazard renderings, randomly ordered and triple-rated by three independent annotators on the four-criterion rubric of Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Realism Rubric ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>—and an LLM-judge analysis on the <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> subset that pairs realism with per-sample cross-model ASR. The defense fails for two independent reasons: <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> renders more plausibly than the strongest prior attack, and within <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> a sample’s plausibility does not predict whether it succeeds.</p>
</div>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span><span id="S4.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE<span id="S4.T2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is rated more realistic than AgentHazard on every criterion (overall <math id="S4.T2.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.02</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S4.T2.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.52</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.52</annotation></semantics></math> on the <math id="S4.T2.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.T2.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> rubric, Mann–Whitney <math id="S4.T2.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></span> Mean human realism on the 200-sample subset (triple-rated; rubric in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Realism Rubric ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>). <em id="S4.T2.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="S4.T2.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math></em>: inter-annotator agreement; <em id="S4.T2.9" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="S4.T2.m43" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math></em>: human–LLM rank correlation. <span id="S4.T2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> = more realistic method.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE<span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is more plausible than AgentHazard under human rating.</span></span> On the deidentified <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n{=}200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n{=}200</annotation></semantics></math> subset (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 RQ2: Stealth ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> reaches mean realism <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.02</annotation></semantics></math> versus AgentHazard’s <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.52</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.52</annotation></semantics></math>, a <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.50</annotation></semantics></math> gap on the <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> rubric that is significant under a two-sided Mann–Whitney <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> test (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U{=}6628" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6628</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U{=}6628</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=6.9\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>6.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=6.9\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>). The gap is uniformly positive across all four criteria (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.47" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.47</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.47</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.53" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.53</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.53</annotation></semantics></math>) and, despite weak inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.15</annotation></semantics></math>), remains significant under the noise-robust Mann–Whitney test.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The result defines an effectiveness–plausibility frontier.</span> Read with RQ1, the comparison traces a two-axis frontier: AgentHazard buys per-sample ASR (the <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+21" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>21</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+21</annotation></semantics></math>pp of §<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 RQ1: Generality and determinants ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) at a measurable plausibility cost (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.50</annotation></semantics></math> Likert, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>), while <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span> deliberately stays at the high-plausibility end, within the visual envelope of plausible user-generated content.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Within <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>, realism does not predict success.</span> On the 200-sample LLM-judge subset, per-sample realism and per-sample cross-model ASR (the fraction of the five agents on which the attack succeeds, in the sense of §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Threat Model and Problem Setup ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>) are uncorrelated: Spearman <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.03</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-0.03</annotation></semantics></math> and Pearson <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=-0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=-0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, both indistinguishable from zero (<math id="S4.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&gt;0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&gt;0.5</annotation></semantics></math>). Mean realism is identical for high-ASR (<math id="S4.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 0.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 0.6</annotation></semantics></math>) and low-ASR (<math id="S4.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 0.2</annotation></semantics></math>) samples (both <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.29" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.29</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.29</annotation></semantics></math>; Figure <a href="#A2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ RQ2 (Stealth): ‣ B.5 Per-RQ Procedure ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MIRAGE</span>’s attacks are therefore not concentrated on visually polished samples, and RQ1 effectiveness does not depend on any sample being indistinguishable from a real UI.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visual-quality filtering is therefore insufficient.</span> Because per-sample plausibility carries no information about per-sample success, any usable plausibility threshold rejects only a representative slice of attacks, not the high-ASR ones; visual-quality filtering—the one runtime defense that does not modify the agent stack—is thus ruled out by the data; a lightweight VLM-classifier probe concurs (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Defense Evaluation ‣ MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). Defenses operating on payload semantics, action-grounding constraints, or user-controllable surface remain open.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S4.T3.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.939" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.939</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.939</annotation></semantics></math></td>
